title: Specific Heat Capacity: J/(kg·K), BTU/(lb·°F) and cal/(g·°C)
h1: Specific heat capacity — J/(kg·K), BTU/(lb·°F) and cal/(g·°C)
description: Water: 4186 J/(kg·K) = 1 BTU/(lb·°F) = 1 cal/(g·°C). Three unit systems, one number for water — coincidence baked in.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: Water's specific heat is the reference. Every other material's is quoted as a fraction. Cooling loops sized around wrong units under-deliver by 4×.
body: Specific heat determines how much energy shifts temperature. Water is the universal reference, and the coincidence that its value is close to 1 in three unit systems keeps confusion alive.
Water: 4186 J/(kg·K). Ice: 2100. Steam: 2000. Ethylene glycol: 2400. Aluminium: 900. Copper: 385. Iron: 449. Air (const. P): 1005. Concrete: 880.

Cooling load 100 kW, ΔT 6 °C, water. ṁ = Q/(c ΔT) = 100 000 / (4186 × 6) = 3.98 kg/s ≈ 240 L/min. Use glycol (c = 3600) and flow rises to 4.63 kg/s — 16% more. Miss the glycol correction and the coil is 16% undersized.
Water is 4186 J/(kg·K). Copper is 385. Miss the factor of 10 and duct/pipe sizing is nonsense.

faqs.a: Weakly — for gases, cp shifts with temperature. For solids and liquids, essentially constant over a working range.
cp = at constant pressure, cv = at constant volume. For solids and liquids they are ~identical; for gases cp = cv + R (per mole).
